The intellectual journal that Carl Schmitt kept under the title Glossarium from 1947 to 1958 survives among his papers in the State Archive of North Rhine-Westphalia, Rhineland Department. It consists of five notebooks, which Schmitt called “books,” bound in black board and light-grey half-cloth (RW 0265, Nos. 19607–19611). Books II, III, and V have title labels written by Schmitt himself. Books I–III measure 17 × 21.5 cm, Book IV 13.5 × 20.5 cm, and Book V 15 × 21 cm. Each cloth spine bears a large “G,” the Roman numeral of the volume, and the period it covers. The notebooks were probably first used as household account books by Schmitt’s wife Duška, as a few isolated entries by her suggest.

Glossarium was first published by Duncker & Humblot in 1991, edited by Schmitt’s former student and assistant Eberhard von Medem. The book attracted a great deal of attention because it contains, in concentrated form, the world of thought of the later Carl Schmitt. These thoughts also appear almost completely unfiltered: spontaneous, written down in rough form, and expressed with all the peculiarities and resentments of an author who had been excluded from academic life but remained fully aware of his own importance.

The text published in 1991, however, had not always been edited with the necessary care, and this in turn encouraged mistaken interpretations. One example is the entry for 25 September 1947, where the edition did not clearly distinguish between a quotation from Peter F. Drucker and Carl Schmitt’s own opinion. Inconsistencies and misreadings were soon discovered as well. The Schmitt scholar Piet Tommissen alone produced a twenty-page list of corrections.

Above all, however, the edition remained unsatisfactory because it contained only the first three books and left out the final two. Eberhard von Medem explained this in his preface by arguing that the quality of Glossarium declined with Book IV. There is only one limited sense in which this is true: the entries become less dense. Their character does not change. Books IV and V are intellectual journals just as much as the earlier books. They are an inseparable part of Glossarium and cannot simply be left out.

The present edition is therefore not merely a corrected second edition of the 1991 publication. It is a complete new transcription of all five books of Glossarium, prepared directly from the manuscripts. It also reproduces in full the increasingly numerous newspaper clippings that Schmitt pasted into the final two books and annotated by hand.

Eberhard von Medem’s main aim had been to provide a smoothly readable text. For that reason, he skipped passages he could not decipher, smoothed out confused passages, or replaced them with conjectures that were not identified as such.
The present edition takes a different approach. It does not claim to be a full historical-critical edition, but it does aim to reproduce the text as accurately and completely as possible.

Schmitt was capable of polished prose of an almost literary quality. But even he had to work on his writing. It is obvious that something written quickly “in a notebook” had not received the author’s final approval and therefore could not possess the same aesthetic and stylistic quality as his published books and essays.

We have naturally made no attempt to change this. Occasional roughness, as well as isolated incomplete sentences or sentences whose grammar breaks off midway, have been left as they appear in the manuscript.

Writing in a notebook also means that one makes no special effort to produce beautiful handwriting. This can be seen again and again in the manuscript of Glossarium. Schmitt often threw something quickly onto the page and was satisfied as long as he himself could read it.

There is an additional difficulty: Schmitt used several different styles of handwriting. Alongside the German Kurrent script he had learned at school—which he also uses for most of Glossarium—there is a flowing and highly legible Latin script of the kind found in his letters. He also occasionally used the much harder-to-decipher Gabelsberger shorthand, though only to a limited extent.
The manuscript is also full of corrections, overwritten words, insertions, and marginal notes whose exact place in the text is not always clear. Passages were sometimes rearranged as well.
Schmitt normally wrote in dark-blue ink, but there are also entries in a lighter blue, as well as passages written in pencil or red pencil. These differences point to different times of composition.

As with his diaries, Carl Schmitt repeatedly returned to the notebooks of Glossarium. He deleted text, wrote over it, and added new material. In most cases, it is impossible to date these later additions more precisely. The manuscript therefore contains several chronological layers.
Because of the state of the manuscript, the text cannot always be transcribed with certainty.

Unreadable passages are marked by three dots inside angle brackets. Uncertain readings and editorial conjectures are also marked with angle brackets. Occasional additions by the editors, by contrast, appear inside square brackets.
This method comes at the expense of smooth reading, but that is the price of accuracy.

The shorthand passages that von Medem had transcribed with the help of his expert Heinrich Mauermann have been adopted without being checked again. The shorthand passages omitted from von Medem’s edition—and there are quite a few of them—were transcribed shortly before his death by Hans Gebhardt, wherever he was able to decipher them.
The punctuation of the original reflects the fact that Schmitt was writing rough notes and is often highly individual.

He very frequently separates parts of a sentence, or even complete sentences, with semicolons. Quotation marks are often missing altogether. Sometimes Schmitt puts an opening quotation mark at the beginning but no closing quotation mark at the end. He also switches between German and French quotation marks.

In the present edition, German quotation marks are used throughout. They have only occasionally been supplied where the absence of quotation marks could create confusion—as in the Peter Drucker quotation mentioned above.
Schmitt’s use of upper- and lowercase letters does not always match present-day practice. His peculiarities have normally been preserved. His spelling has also been preserved.

Occasional simple spelling mistakes have nevertheless been corrected without comment. A few archaic forms—such as “Huppe” instead of “Hupe,” “abluxen” instead of “abluchsen,” and “allmählig” instead of “allmählich”—have been modernized.
Abbreviations are expanded in square brackets unless they can be assumed to be generally understood.
The many passages in foreign languages are translated in the commentary appendix, but only when they are in ancient languages, namely Greek and Latin.
Schmitt wrote the names of books of the Bible in several different ways. In this edition they are cited using the abbreviations of the Theologische Realenzyklopädie.
Because Carl Schmitt repeatedly returned to Glossarium, the entire manuscript is covered with marginal cross-references, and these become increasingly frequent toward the end.
They are reproduced in the printed text as footnotes.

Schmitt normally made these cross-references by date, although he sometimes referred instead to a manuscript page number. Since such manuscript page numbers are of no use to the reader, they have been converted in square brackets either into dates or into printed page references.

The title labels and endpapers of the individual volumes contain several different titles written by Schmitt. These formulations reveal how he understood the work, and they are therefore reproduced in the appendix.
It seems that Glossarium only gradually took shape in the author’s mind—in a status nascendi, a state of coming into being.

Pages 1 to 9 of the first book show Schmitt’s thoughts gradually taking form through the very act of writing. What begins as little more than notes and extracts from books soon condenses into original thought.
According to a note Schmitt wrote on the endpaper, Glossarium proper was only meant to begin on page 10.

On the reverse of folio 66 of Book I—page 386 in the printed text—there is a dated entry that chronologically belongs before the true beginning of the main text. It has therefore been placed within the chronology of pages 1 to 9.
There are also notes on the endpapers of all five volumes. All of these entries are reproduced in an appendix.
In Book III, after folio 75, there is a loose sheet containing a shorthand note. It is extremely difficult to decipher and has therefore not been included here.
Schmitt wrote Glossarium in longhand. This is striking because, unlike Glossarium, the diaries he kept throughout his life were not written this way.
Von Medem concluded from this that Schmitt must have been thinking about publication.

The editors of the present edition find this unlikely because of the unfinished state of the text described above. Carl Schmitt was far too conscious a stylist to have sent the manuscript to a publisher in this form.
The use of longhand may instead suggest that Schmitt wanted his thoughts to remain accessible to a limited circle of family members and close friends.
Deciding how much commentary to provide was not easy.
